source.title: Dimensional Collapse in Transformer Attention Outputs: A Challenge for Sparse Dictionary Learning
source.authors: Junxuan Wang; Xu-Yang Ge; Wentao Shu; Zheng-Fu He; Xi-Peng Qiu

page_placements.theme: Dense structure, anisotropy and privileged representation bases

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse dictionary learning to LLM activations and reports SAE reconstruction results in that setting, but does not test the toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper measures activation effective rank and SAE reconstruction, not whether underlying features are nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, distributed across neurons, or canonical units. Its related-work section explicitly distinguishes SAE applications from direct tests of the superposition hypothesis. Low-rankness and dead-feature findings are recorded as related results, not as tests of those feature-geometry claims.
record.test_reason: The paper uses SAEs as a tool and reports its own initialization method (ASI) against TopK and AuxK baselines: dead features, NMSE and delta LM loss. It does not test whether features are superposed, distributed across neurons, or recovered as true model features. The authors say SAE applications 'do not constitute direct hypothesis tests' of superposition. The low-rank activation findings are a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that attention outputs are confined to a low-rank subspace (about 60% effective rank vs about 90% for MLP outputs and the residual stream). They say this holds across models and datasets and is shaped largely by W_O. The abstract and conclusion call low rank 'a key cause' of dead features, while the Discussion concedes the causal mechanism is unresolved. ASI improves reconstruction and, combined with SparseAdam, cuts dead features from 87% to below 1% at 1M features. ASI gives little gain on near-full-rank activations and in high-initial-L0 JumpReLU or K-annealing regimes.
record.recipe_differences: Measures LLM activation spectra and trains sparse autoencoders; it does not reproduce the original toy-model feature-sparsity experiments or their feature-direction geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: ASI performance depends on activation rank and training setup: the authors report little improvement for near-full-rank residual activations and for JumpReLU or TopK annealing regimes that remain at high initial sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention outputs have an effective rank of about 60% of dimension, versus about 90% for MLP outputs and the residual stream. This holds across GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen3, Pythia and several datasets. The authors attribute it largely to the output projection W_O.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention-output activations in LLMs occupy a markedly lower-effective-rank subspace than MLP outputs or the residual stream.

fits_no_version.finding: About 39% of attention-output singular components recover over 99% of downstream loss, versus about 95–97% for MLP outputs and the residual stream.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention-output information is functionally concentrated in a compact subspace.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on lower-effective-rank sites have more dead features. Examples: layer 15 attention 79.86% vs residual 45.70% at 32k features, L0=32 (Table 1). The authors leave the causal mechanism unresolved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low effective rank of activations correlates with SAE dead-feature prevalence.

record.problems: The paper reports a correlation between effective rank and dead features but says the causal mechanism is unresolved. Some broad cross-model and cross-dataset results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. SAE reconstruction does not establish recovery of ground-truth model features.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix tables and figures report additional dead-feature rates, layer/model/dataset comparisons, and SAE training metrics. They were not extracted because they concern initialization and dead-feature outcomes rather than a tested claim version; the main activation-geometry and representative SAE reconstruction results are retained.

untested.parts: No toy models, no feature-sparsity sweep, no measurement of overlap or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or of feature importance.
No analysis of the origins of polysemantic neurons.
SAE reconstruction is reported only as a method comparison. There is no test that features are distributed across neurons or that sparse features are genuinely recovered.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicality of SAE features. The monosemanticity comparison (Appendix N) is between two SAE initializations only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. They rested on the study's own method-vs-baseline reconstruction numbers, which cannot bear on whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features. Appendix N reports blinded monosemanticity scores for 50 features per SAE: ASI 31/50 and TopK 30/50 scored 4–5, with no significant difference. It also finds almost no alive features aligned with the 'dead subspace'. These are SAE-quality comparisons between initializations, not tests of V4 or V5, so they are not added as rows. The paper mentions attention-head superposition only as an intuitive explanation for subspace overlap and does not test it.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks, feature overlap or near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular feature geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for limited capacity or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE reconstruction on LLM activations, but does not test whether features are distributed across many neurons or establish recovery of ground-truth model features.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; its semantic-consistency comparison does not establish those properties.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: It uses sparse dictionary learning motivated by superposition. Its reconstruction, dead-feature and comparative feature-quality evaluations do not establish overlapping underlying features or complete, stable, canonical dictionary units.

tranche.reason: The paper measures activation spectra and evaluates its SAE initialization method. These are related constructs and method-performance results, rather than tests of the catalog's superposition claim versions.

source_check.notes: Appendix N evaluates monosemanticity to compare SAE variants and reports no significant difference; it does not validate recovered features as underlying model units. Section 6 explicitly leaves the causal mechanism linking low rank and dead features unresolved.

statements.correction: Section 4.3: attention effective rank around 60%; MLP and residual stream around 90%. Appendix D, Figure 10c, Qwen3-8B on SlimPajamaGithub: effective dimensionalities attention=2410, MLP=3495, residual=2000. Figure 10d, Qwen3-4B on SlimPajama: attention=1122, MLP=1485, residual=990. Residual effective dimensionality is below attention in both settings.
statements.problem: The abstract and Section 4.3 give the approximate 60%/90% summary, but extending it across all reported settings overlooks substantial exceptions in Appendix D.
